We are particularly unhappy with that part of the bill which provides that once a bilingual district has been set up it will remain a bilingual district even though its population changes. That is firmly spelled out in the bill. Once a bilingual district, always a bilingual district-that is what the bill says. In these days people move about quickly and easily from one area to another. We can easily conceive of a situation in which, over a 15 year period, the 10 per cent of the people speaking French in a bilingual area may, because of their mobility and changing circumstances, move away from the area and leave behind, say, 1 per cent of the total population of the area which can speak French. In other words, only 1 per cent of those in the bilingual district will speak French-and the argument is equally applicable to English speaking people in a French area-but the bilingual district will still remain a bilingual district. The government will still have to supply bilingual services in the area for the entire population, even though 1 per cent of the population speaks one of the official languages and 99 per cent speaks the other. We feel that is not right.
This matter was mentioned in committee. We feel that it entails a waste of the taxpayers' money. We do not object to money being spent on bilingual services where they are required and where they will be used. We see some very grave and serious dangers arising if this bill is not properly administered. In committee we sought to remedy some of the rather glaring weak spots in the bill in terms of its administrative provisions. It is with some justifiable pride that I say that some of the proposals we made in the committee were accepted. I should like briefly to review for the house the proposals that were made by us in committee and which the government members of the committee as well as the committee as a whole saw fit to accept.
Clause 15 as originally drafted set up the bilingual districts advisory board. An examination of the original clause 15 revealed that the advisory board was given the power to determine whether or not a certain area should be classified as a bilingual district, and this determination could be made without holding a public hearing. We felt that this function was important enough to warrant a public hearing in the area concerned before that determination was made. We, therefore, submitted a proposal to the committee which the committee accepted. As a result, before determining that a given area shall be classified as a bilingual district, the bilingual districts advisory board must now hold at least one public hearing in that area, at which hearing organizations and individuals are free to make known their views.
Clause 24 of the original bill authorized the commissioner of official languages-and make no mistake about it, Mr. Speaker; this man is given great powers-not only to carry out the duties assigned to him under the languages bill, but also, the original bill states, to:
-carry out such other assignments and engage in such other activities as may be authorized by the Governor in Council.
Official Languages
We conceived that to mean that, if the Governor in Council saw fit he could authorize this commissioner to carry out practically any kind of investigation, even though it may not be related to his duties under the official languages act. Therefore, we asked the committee, and the committee agreed, to include the word "related", in the clause, and now the bill provides that the commissioner can carry out only those assignments that are related to the official languages act which may be authorized by the Governor in Council.
Clause 25 of the original bill gave the commissioner power to interfere in the affairs of parliament. We felt that this was much too broad a power to give the commissioner and so we had the clause amended. As a result of our amendment, his power now extends only to the institutions of the parliament of Canada and not to the parliament of Canada itself.
Clause 26 (5) as originally drafted provided that, if the commissioner thought fit, he could give his reasons for any decision that he made. For example, if a complaint were made against a department of government or an individual, the commissioner would hold a hearing; but under the bill as originally drafted the commissioner was not required to make his decision known to the department of government or individual concerned. We suggested, and I think properly suggested because the committee accepted our suggestion, that the words "if he thinks fit" should be dropped. As a result of our proposal in committee, the commissioner is now required to make known the reasons for his decision. Before that the bill said the commissioner did not have to inform the complainant of the reasons for his decision. Now, the commissioner is required to notify not only the complainant but also the people complained against of the reasons for his decision. We were happy indeed that the minister and the committee went as far as they did in meeting our suggestions in committee. We were glad to see the changes brought in; nevertheless, we still feel that other changes to the bill could have been made to improve it. We tried to introduce those changes by bringing amendments before this house, but unfortunately they did not carry.

As I said earlier, the bill is unfortunately much misunderstood throughout the country. With all due respect, I suggest that responsibility for this situation lies at the doorstep of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) whose complete failure to engage personally in a dialogue with the Canadian people about this measure is a major factor in permitting the amount of misunderstanding which exists today.
The Prime Minister would like to blame the press. But I think the press has done an excellent job in trying to get across to the Canadian people the principles embodied in this bill. The people of Canada did not necessarily want to hear from the press. So many of the things they see in the press they take with a grain of salt. They wanted to hear these things from the lips of the Prime Minister of Canada. He was the man who carried the responsibility for promoting the principles of the official languages bill. I cannot for the life of me understand why he did not promote the measure to a greater extent. Surely, there is nothing in the bill of which he need be ashamed. As far as the principle is concerned, he can be proud of it. Why he did not go out and properly explain the purpose of the measure to the people of Canada, thus avoiding all the confusion and misunderstanding which now exists in the minds of the people, is beyond my comprehension. We on this side continue to be baffled by the Prime Minister's gross neglect in this respect.

We know he cares about this measure. At least, I feel he does. He was the man who conceived it. Why has he not explained it to the people personally? He could have done much to end the unhappiness felt in some parts of our country where this bill has been misinterpreted and misunderstood. The blame for the present situation lies directly on the doorstep of the Prime Minister of Canada. He could have made a major contribution to Canadian unity during the past few weeks by explaining to the people of this country what this bill is all about. Unfortunately, the Prime Minister chose not to do this. Indeed, it seems to us that at times the Prime Minister prefers to leave to the opposition parties the task of trying to explain this government measure. I suggest that is a very strange situation.

Far too many commentators, both in the press and on the radio, have treated this bill as an ethnic measure, as a racist bill. This bill does not deal with race but with language; let that be very clearly understood. This bill deals with two great linguistic cultures, with a great partnership of two groups of people, each with its hopes and fears, its aspirations, its pride in the other and faith in the future, in terms of two tongues, two languages. I submit the so-called third force is not a third force; its members belong to one of two great, co-equal first forces. We in this country are united by a common language, which is one of the two official languages. No Canadian can be properly classed as a third class citizen or even as a second class citizen in so far as his rights, his privileges and his citizenship are concerned.
If this bill were concerned with the dominance of French-speaking Canadians, or with those who are commonly referred to as WASPS, over other kinds of Canadians, as some who misunderstand the bill would have us believe, then the bill would not receive support from the members of this party. Neither would it be supported by those of Scottish, Irish or Welsh origin or by those of non-Protestant religious faith. The members of this party are proud to rank in exactly the same order of equality as all other Canadians who speak the French or English languages, regardless of place of birth or line of descent.

I believe it is admitted by all fairminded people that as a general rule we have got along very well together in the past. There have been differences, as naturally there are bound to be, and this bill may strengthen our determination to live happily with each other. Such an objective, and I take this to be the objective of the bill, certainly cannot be opposed, and it is simply because of that objective that I and the party I have the honour to represent support the principle embodied in this bill.
To further the determination of the English and French speaking peoples to live happily together, the bill seeks to ensure that no matter which of the two official languages Canadians speak they will be able to enjoy the services of the government in their own language. Surely no fairminded person can take any serious exception to that. The bill directs federal government agencies to provide public services in both languages in areas which have been determined by the advisory board to be bilingual, that is, where at least 10 per cent of the people living in these areas speak either French or English or, in other areas, where in the opinion of the commissioner it is practical to have bilingualism. Under the bill public services in both languages will be provided wherever there are enough speakers of both languages to make the use of those languages a workable and worth-while objective. As legislators I think we will agree it is the very essence of good government to deal with all citizens in ways which are clear and unambiguous1, and to the extent that this bill promotes that object we support it.

The Canadian confederation will work only if the French-Canadian people do not feel threatened in their development as such.

As I said a moment ago, one of the greatest problems facing the public service is the expression of viewpoints on important issues of this kind. I am very conscious of this problem. If I may be permitted a personal reference I might explain to the house something which I attempted to do in April of this year. When my constituency association had its annual meeting, arrangements were made for a discussion on the policy of bilingualism. That meeting was attended by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister and the executive secretary of the Professional Institute of the Public Service of Canada.
During that discussion two points were made which I think are important to record at this time. The first point was that the Professional Institute, and I think other organizations representing public servants, felt that the policy as it had developed up to that time had not really protected unilingual civil servants of long experience and service in the way this was contemplated in Mr. Pearson's statement. The other point, which is equally important, is that the staff associations representing the public service were very definitely of the opinion that there had not been consultation between them and the authorities of the government of Canada in respect of the implementation of this policy, as was contemplated in the statement of Mr. Pearson.
The position in which we now find ourselves is that the policy of bilingualism in the public service, which, as the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) pointed out the other night, had been expressed in a previous statute, the Public Service Employment Act passed in 1967, will now receive wider application and greater authority by virtue of the passage of this bill. It seems to me quite clear that as we embark upon this very great enterprise of providing greater access to our public institutions to those people speaking either French or English, we must be sure that this aim or policy is not in any sense defeated by the means used to implement it. It is my view that the success of this policy over the next few years and, indeed, over a longer period of time, will depend to a very considerable extent upon the degree of support and confidence it enlists from the public service.
I see no evidence now that it will not have the support and confidence of the type required. There is no evidence that the authorities of the government responsible for

the administration of this policy will be anything but diligent in an effort to make sure that the basic principles of equity and justice, implicit in Mr. Pearson's remarks, are continued in the forefront of the application of the policy.
Now that we have had some experience with the application of this policy and how it can be made effective by virtue of regulations and procedures within the public service, I believe the time has come to review the position of public servants with seniority and experience. Certainly it seems to me that in any case where bilingualism is not an absolute requisite for a particular position in the public service, any preference or special points given to persons with bilingual capability should be balanced off in the case of experienced unilingual civil servants by a formula which takes into account their years of service.

The first thing I should like to say is that, as all hon. members know, the public service of Canada is in a unique position in relation to this legislation and indeed in relation to any general policy expounded by the various governments of this country. Having said that, I should also like to express the opinion that we in this parliament are under a special obligation toward the members of the public service who in a very real sense are our employees. These are people who rightfully look not only to government but to parliamentarians to protect them. Indeed, I think it is fair to say-and one could put it stronger than that by saying it is perfectly evident-that the public service of Canada has been one of the greatest unifying forces in the nation. There are many people here in this chamber and certainly in this city who like myself came originally from the far regions of Canada to Ottawa to work for the public service. subsubtopic: SUPPORT BY DR. O. M. SOLANDT OF BELL CANADA RATE INCREASE
speechtext: May I ask the minister whether he has considered the propriety of the chairman of a government board appearing before another public body at the request of, and in support of, necessarily, a private or public corporation asking for favours from that public body?

subsubtopic: SUPPORT BY DR. O. M. SOLANDT OF BELL CANADA RATE INCREASE
speechtext: I am not sure I would agree that the applicant in this case was seeking favours. I reject the dialectic used by the hon. member. Dr. Solandt appeared at the request of Bell Telephone Company to offer expert evidence in relation to the research and development effort being put forward by Bell. He was not asked to address himself, nor did he address himself, to the question whether or not a rate increase was necessary or desirable.

They have complained about the fact that there are not enough of them to do the increasingly important and expanding job. Why it has taken the department until now to realize that they have to start getting more people and training them for this important job, God only knows. I just do not understand this long delay. I hope that the minister and the department this time will really undertake the job of recruitment and training with an eye to the next decade or so, because the job is an important one, the training requires time, and I hope there will be a sufficient work force to do the job properly.
The second point I want to make is that I do not know why the second volume of the Robinson report is being tabled only today. I suppose it has only recently been received. As a matter of fact, I am ashamed to admit that I had forgotten there was a second volume which parliament had not yet seen, even though it is almost three years since Judge Robinson was appointed. I hope that the figure of 75 per cent of the recommendations which have been implemented is not merely a quantitive figure but also a qualitative one. You can implement niggling things that do not mean anything and have them add up to 75 per cent. From what air traffic controllers have told me I have a strong suspicion that the arithmetic is of that kind and that some of the really important matters about which Judge Robinson was concerned have not yet been implemented.
Finally, I want to draw to the minister's attention the fact that there is still a great deal of objection from residents in the area to the proposed extension of one of the Toronto runways, and those of us in the Toronto area at least who are in the house have received briefs from an association that is deeply concerned about that. I hope the minister will meet with these people and satisfy them that whatever is to be done is essential, necessary, and will not be done at the expense of their comfort and welfare.
The matter of the air traffic controllers has taken far too long, for a start at least, to give us a sufficient work force to assure not only the safety of the people travelling by air but also to ensure that the welfare of the air traffic controllers themselves will be protected and that their lives will not be darkened by overwork and overanxiety.

subsubtopic: LETTER FROM DR. O. M. SOLANDT RESPECTING SCIENCE POLICY
speechtext: I think Dr. Solandt was addressing himself rather more to the general problem of the lack of adequate statistics in Canada relating to expenditures on research and development.
